analysis.one_liner: Bars mortgage servicers from foreclosing on homeowners before reviewing them for loan modifications.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a vote: introduced in May 2011 with 17 bipartisan cosponsors, it sat in the Senate Banking Committee until the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targeted a practice in the mortgage servicing industry known as dual tracking: while a homeowner was being strung along on a loan modification application, the servicer could simultaneously push the foreclosure forward. It would have required every servicer to give each struggling borrower one named case manager with real decision-making authority, barred servicers from starting a foreclosure until they had fully reviewed the borrower's file and offered any modification the borrower qualified for, suspended foreclosures already underway until that review was done, and required an independent review before telling a borrower they were ineligible. A servicer that violated the rules could not proceed with the foreclosure until it came back into compliance [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners in default or at risk of default, who would have gotten a single accountable contact at their servicer, a complete eligibility review before any foreclosure could start, and a pause on foreclosures already in motion until that review was finished [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Each borrower seeking a loan modification or alternative to foreclosure would be assigned one case manager who handles all communication and has the authority to decide eligibility, replacing the common experience of calling repeatedly and getting a different, uninformed person each time [S3].

Servicers could not start a foreclosure until they completed a full file review, made documented outreach efforts to reach the borrower, and offered any modification or alternative the borrower qualified for [S2] [S3].

Foreclosures already underway when the law took effect would have to be suspended — no foreclosure notices, no scheduled sales, no final judgments — until the review was completed and any eligible borrower was offered help [S3].
Before a servicer could tell a borrower they were ineligible, an independent reviewer would have to examine the file and make the eligibility call [S2] [S3].
A violation of the act would bar the foreclosure action itself, though a servicer that later complied could proceed anyway [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage servicers — largely units of the largest banks — would bear the cost of staffing case managers, completing file reviews before foreclosing, halting foreclosures already in progress, and paying for independent reviews. Investors holding defaulted mortgages would also wait longer for resolution on nonperforming loans [S3].

drawbacks.text: The 'independent reviewer' does not have to be truly independent: the bill's own definition allows a division inside the servicer itself, as long as it sits under different immediate supervision from the division handling modification applications [S3].
A servicer that violates the rules can still proceed with the foreclosure once it comes into compliance, so the penalty is delay rather than a true bar [S3].

Suspending every foreclosure initiated before enactment would have lengthened timelines on genuinely hopeless defaults, which delays resolution for investors and can prolong uncertainty for neighborhoods with vacant properties — though the bill carves out exceptions for abandoned homes and unreachable borrowers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection — no foreclosure before a real eligibility review and a single accountable contact — would have directly addressed the dual-tracking abuses homeowners were experiencing after the housing crash, and the burden falls on an industry whose foreclosure-fee revenue was part of the problem. The bill is weakened by design compromises: the independent review can happen inside the servicer's own walls, and violations are curable with no lasting consequence. Still, the protections are real, and the main objection (slower foreclosures) comes with explicit escape valves for abandoned properties and unresponsive borrowers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the Regulation of Mortgage Servicing Act of 2011 on May 12, 2011, with an initial group of cosponsors including Republican Olympia Snowe and Independent Bernie Sanders [S3] [S5].
Seventeen senators cosponsored the bill: 15 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day of introduction [S5].
No further action of any kind — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — is recorded for the remainder of the 112th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage servicers and the large banks behind them, which avoided the case-manager, pre-foreclosure-review, and suspension requirements; homeowners in default got no help from this bill.

sides.party_line_note: Seventeen senators signed on — 15 Democrats, 1 Republican (Snowe of Maine), and 1 Independent (Sanders of Vermont) — and no vote was ever held, so the chamber never split on it.

industries.industry: Mortgage servicers (largely units of the biggest banks)
industries.note: The bill would have forced servicers to stop foreclosing while reviewing borrowers for modifications, staff a decision-making case manager for every distressed borrower, and suspend foreclosures already underway. Servicers had been collecting fees and pushing properties to sale during exactly the period the bill would have paused, so the requirements came at a direct cost to that revenue stream.

Longer pre-foreclosure review periods mean defaulted loans stay unresolved longer, extending the time before investors recover on nonperforming mortgages. The bill's exceptions for abandoned properties and unreachable borrowers limit but do not eliminate the delay.
